summary:
NEXUS is an AI-powered desktop mission trainer that puts students in command of a real lunar or Martian outpost. Players balance life support, power, food, water, and radiation shielding across 30 simulated mission days, experiencing firsthand the trade-offs that determine whether a crew survives or fails.

The simulation engine runs on deterministic code — no AI invents outcomes or numbers. The AI copilot, NEXUS, answers science questions using Retrieval-Augmented Generation over four real NASA and NOAA documents, citing every answer to its source. When a solar particle event hits or a scrubber fails, the player must decide under pressure, and NEXUS explains the real science behind the consequence.

NEXUS addresses the challenge by making space engineering trade-offs tangible and interactive. It runs fully offline, works for any age or background, and was built in Accra, Ghana, to show that the next generation of space explorers can come from anywhere on Earth.
details:
What it does:

NEXUS is a resource-management game and science trainer. The player commands a Moon or Mars outpost for 30 days, allocating crew effort daily across power, oxygen, water, food, and radiation shielding. Random events (solar particle events, scrubber faults, crop blights, micrometeoroid strikes, dust storms) force decisions. The simulation code applies fixed consequences — no AI decides outcomes. At the end, the player sees whether the mission succeeded or failed and why.

How it works:

The simulation engine (Python) runs a deterministic day cycle. Each day, resources are consumed and produced based on the player's allocation. Events are triggered probabilistically and resolved by player choice from three fixed options. The AI copilot answers science questions using RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) over four NASA and NOAA documents indexed in ChromaDB. Every answer cites its source document and page number. If the answer is not in the documents, NEXUS says so. The app runs fully offline except for the Groq LLM answer step, which falls back to retrieved text with citations if the internet is unavailable.

Benefits and impact:

NEXUS makes the engineering trade-offs of space exploration tangible for students of any age or background. It teaches that you cannot maximise everything, that decisions have cascading consequences, and that real NASA science underpins every game mechanic. It is accessible locally and globally, runs on any Windows desktop, and requires no specialist hardware.

Tools and languages:

Python 3.13, PyQt6 (desktop UI), ChromaDB (vector database for RAG), pymupdf4llm (PDF parsing), Groq API (LLM and speech transcription, model openai/gpt-oss-120b, transcription whisper-large-v3-turbo), vosk (offline wake-word detection), hashlib (local profile password hashing). Outpost artwork generated with Gemini Image Generation. Development assisted by GitHub Copilot and Claude (Anthropic).

Creativity and considerations:

The Mars communication delay mechanic (3 to 22 simulated minutes one-way) forces the player to decide alone, teaching the autonomy required for deep-space missions. The outpost scene reacts to the simulation state: resource hotspots change colour and flash on matching events. All simulation values are clearly labelled as such. No invented numbers, no false live-data claims. Built by a two-person team in Accra, Ghana, for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.
